blocks.text: “Good Heaven, my dear little woman,” said he, “how did you get here? Who could have expected to see you! Is nothing wrong? Is Ada well?”
“Ah!” he said, leaning back in his chair. “My poor cousin! I was writing to you, Esther.”
How worn and tired he looked, even in the full strength of his handsome youth! He was leaning back in his chair, crushing a closely written sheet of paper in his hand.
“Have you taken all the trouble to write that? And am I not going to read it after all?” I asked.
“Oh my dear,” he answered, with a hopeless movement of his hand. “You can read it in the whole room. It is all over here.”
I gently begged him not to lose hope. I told him that I had heard by chance that he was in difficulty. I had come to talk with him about what could best be done.

“That is like you, Esther. But it is useless, and so it is not like you!” he said with a sad smile. “I am away on leave today—I should have been gone in another hour. That is meant to smooth things over, for my selling out—giving up my place in the army. Well! Let the past be the past. So this profession follows all the others. I only need to have been in the church, and then I would have tried every profession there is.”
“Richard,” I urged, “it is not so hopeless as that?”

“Esther,” he answered, “it is indeed. I am so close to disgrace that the people who are put in authority over me (as the catechism says) would much rather be without me than with me. And they are right. Leave aside my debts, and the people who keep coming to demand payment, and all such problems. Even so, I am not fit even for this job. I have no care, no mind, no heart, no soul, except for one thing. Why, if this bubble had not burst now,” he said, tearing the letter he had written into small pieces and throwing them away a few at a time in a gloomy way, “how could I have gone abroad? I would certainly have been ordered abroad; but how could I have gone? With my experience of that thing, how could I trust even Vholes unless I was right there behind him?”
I suppose he knew from my face what I was about to say. But he caught the hand I had laid on his arm, and touched my own lips with it, to stop me from going on.

“No, Dame Durden! There are two subjects I forbid—I must forbid. The first is John Jarndyce. The second, you know what. Call it madness, and I tell you I can't help it now, and I can't be sane. But it is no such thing; it is the one goal I have to follow. It is a pity I was ever persuaded to turn away from my road for anything else. It would be wisdom to give it up now, after all the time, worry and effort I have spent on it! Oh yes, true wisdom. It would be very pleasant, too, for some people; but I never will.”

He was in such a mood that I thought it best not to oppose him. Opposing him would only make him more determined (if anything could make him more determined). I took out Ada's letter and put it in his hand.
“Am I to read it now?” he asked.

When I told him yes, he laid it on the table, rested his head on his hand, and began. He had not read far when he rested his head on both hands—to hide his face from me. After a little while he stood up, as if the light were bad, and went to the window. He finished reading it there, with his back to me. After he had finished and had folded it up, he stood there for some minutes with the letter in his hand. When he came back to his chair, I saw tears in his eyes.
“Of course, Esther, you know what she says here?” He spoke in a softened voice, and kissed the letter as he asked me.

“She offers me,” he went on, tapping his foot on the floor, “the little inheritance that she is certain to receive so soon. It is just as little and as much as what I have wasted. And she begs and prays me to take it, to put myself right with it, and to stay in the army.”
